title: Is Hell Real, and Is It Fair?
excerpt: The old objection to hell is that no short life could deserve an endless punishment. The church has given three answers to it, and Jesus said more about the fairness of judgment than either side of the argument tends to remember.
body:
Three people can ask whether hell is fair and mean three different things. One is a man whose father has just died. The father was honest in business and gentle with his grandchildren, and for eighty-one years he was politely uninterested in God, and the son can't make the word hell fit the man he knew. One is a woman who was harmed as a girl by someone who died old and admired, with a full church at his funeral. She isn't asking whether judgment is too severe. She is asking whether there will be any. And one is a student who has done the sum that anyone can do: seventy or eighty years of wrongdoing on one side, and on the other a punishment that never ends.

The student's sum is the objection in its plainest form. Justice means that a punishment fits the wrong. A life lasts some decades, and the harm done in it, however great, comes to an end. Endless suffering has no end. A God who imposed it would be doing wrong, and a God who loved the people he made wouldn't impose it in any case. John Stuart Mill wrote in 1865 that he would call no being good who wasn't good in the sense we mean when we use the word of one another, and that if the price of saying so were hell, "to hell I will go."

Christians did not first hear this from their critics. Augustine, writing in North Africa in the 420s, reports that some people "think it unjust that any man be doomed to an eternal punishment for sins which, no matter how great they were, were perpetrated in a brief space of time." Eight centuries later Thomas Aquinas wrote the objection into his own textbook before he tried to answer it: "a just punishment is equal to the fault, since justice is equality." Long before either of them the prophet Ezekiel wrote down what his own people were saying: "Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just'" (Ezekiel 18:25). The question is as old as the teaching.

Nothing in this essay says where any person is or will be. Nobody writing it or reading it has been given that knowledge.

If you're grieving as you read this, you don't have to resolve any of it before you're allowed to pray. Bring the question to God in whatever words you have; the psalms give you permission. Bring it to a person too, a friend or a pastor who will sit with you. If you have started to wonder whether you want to go on living, reach out today: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This essay can't counsel you, but [Find Help](/help) has other lines you can call and a page for grief.

## What the Objection Gets Right

The objection's first premise is the Bible's own. The law of Moses told judges to sentence a guilty man "in proportion to his offense," and then it set a ceiling: "Forty stripes may be given him, but not more, lest, if one should go on to beat him with more stripes than these, your brother be degraded in your sight" (Deuteronomy 25:2–3). A person who says that punishment must fit the crime has not carried a foreign standard into Scripture.

The objection is also right about some of the church's defenses, which tell us more about the defender's world than about God. When Augustine answers his critics, he points out that no court measures a sentence by the minutes the crime took, and that is true. But one of the examples he gives of a fitting sentence is "a penalty of many years' confinement imposed on the slave who has provoked his master with a word." He doesn't notice what his example shows. Every age's sense of what is fair carries some of that age's cruelty inside it, ours included, and that should make all of us slower to speak for God here.

## What Jesus Said About Fairness

Jesus is the New Testament's chief source on hell, and another essay on this site sets out [his words and the long argument over them](/writing/is-hell-real-and-is-it-forever). What is easy to miss is how much of his teaching about judgment is about whether it will be fair.

He says that it will be measured. In one of his parables the servant who knew what his master wanted and ignored it "will receive a severe beating," while the one "who did not know" will receive "a light beating" (Luke 12:47–48). Then Jesus states the rule that governs both: "Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required" (Luke 12:48).

He says that it will take account of what a person had the chance to know. To the Galilean towns that had watched him work and shrugged, he said that "it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you" (Matthew 11:22), and those were pagan cities. The Study Bible's note on that chapter, on this site, draws the conclusion in six words: judgment "is measured by the light received."

He says that judgment will go by what people did, and that it will surprise them. In his picture of the last day the test is what was done for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner, and both groups are astonished at where they stand. He ends that scene by saying that "these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). He speaks of "a great chasm" fixed after death (Luke 16:26) and of a door that the master of the house "has risen and shut" (Luke 13:25). He taught that judgment would be fair and that it would be final, and he didn't apologize for either.

He said one more thing about fairness, and it cuts the other way. In one of his best-known stories the charge of unfairness comes from people who are angry about a kindness shown to someone else. The workers hired at dawn complain about the ones hired late in the day: "you have made them equal to us" (Matthew 20:12). The owner asks, "do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:15). Jesus expected that when people accused God of unfairness, it would often be mercy they objected to.

## Three Answers to the Sum

Christians who recite the same creeds have answered the student's sum in three ways, and each one denies a different line of it. A longer page on this site, on [how a good God could punish anyone forever](/questions/evil/hell-and-the-justice-of-god), goes through the argument step by step.

The first answer is the one most of the church has given, in the East and in the West. The lost suffer conscious separation from God, and it does not end. The teachers who hold this have never claimed that a lifetime of sins adds up to infinity. Aquinas agrees with the critic that "Punishment is proportionate to sin." What he denies is that sin is only an amount of harm done in an amount of time. Sin, he says, has two sides. It is a grasping at some limited good, and for that side the penalty is limited. It is also "the turning away from the immutable good, which is infinite," a turning from God himself, and the penalty for that side is to lose God. That loss has no measure because of what is lost. He repeats an older argument as well, that an offense is weighed by the one it is committed against, as striking a ruler was a graver thing in his world than striking a private man. And he gives a third, the one modern defenders most often use. A person who has made sin his final aim "has the will to sin, everlastingly." On this account hell is the settled state of a will that goes on refusing. C. S. Lewis put that in one line in 1940: "the doors of hell are locked on the inside."

The same teachers say that the punishment is graded. Augustine wrote that "even the eternal fire will be proportioned to the deserts of the wicked, so that to some it will be more, and to others less painful." And they deny that God enjoys it. "God does not delight in punishments for their own sake," Aquinas says.

This answer has hard questions to face, and its best defenders feel them. We no longer weigh a crime by the rank of the victim. We weigh it by the harm done and by what the person knew, and the son in the first paragraph can't see his father as a man who looked at infinite goodness with open eyes and turned away. It is fair to ask whether a limited creature, half informed and often deceived, can make a refusal that deserves to last forever, and how anyone knows that every lost person will go on refusing. And Paul promises a day when God will be "all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28). An endless suffering has to be fitted somewhere inside that promise.

The second answer accepts the critic's premise about proportion and denies that hell is endless suffering. It is called conditional immortality, or annihilationism, and it holds that the lost finally perish and are no more. Its holders say they are reading the Bible's most common words in their ordinary sense. God "alone has immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16). Eternal life is something he gives to those who "seek for glory and honor and immortality" (Romans 2:7), and Jesus warned of the one "who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28). Paul calls the fate of the lost "eternal destruction" (2 Thessalonians 1:9). They point to Irenaeus, a bishop of the second century, who wrote that "life does not arise from us, nor from our own nature; but it is bestowed according to the grace of God," though how far he would have gone with them is disputed. Its fullest modern statement is a book of 1982 by Edward Fudge, and in 1988 John Stott wrote that he held the view, though tentatively. On this account the punishment is eternal because it is never reversed, and whatever suffering comes before the end can be measured to the person, as the severe beating and the light one suggest.

Its hard questions are textual first. Jesus set "eternal punishment" beside "eternal life" in a single sentence, and Revelation says of the devil, the beast and the false prophet that "they will be tormented day and night forever and ever" (Revelation 20:10). And it meets a fairness question from the opposite side. The woman in the first paragraph may wonder whether ceasing to exist is any judgment at all for a man who wanted only to have his deeds never brought up. Conditionalists reply that he must first stand before the Judge and hear the truth told, and then loses everything there is to lose.

The third answer denies that the loss is final. Origen of Alexandria wrote in the third century that "the end is always like the beginning." A century later Gregory of Nyssa, who helped to defend the creed of Nicaea, looked ahead to a time "when evil shall have been some day annihilated in the long revolutions of the ages," so that "nothing shall be left outside the world of goodness." In its holders' own terms judgment is real and may be terrible, but its purpose is to heal, and a punishment that never ends can never finish healing anyone. They read Paul's sentence that "one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men" (Romans 5:18) as meaning what it says.

The church as a whole has not received this as its teaching. In the sixth century an anathema was pronounced on Origen's doctrine at Constantinople. The Lutheran confession of 1530 rejects the opinion "that there will be an end to the punishments of condemned men and devils," and most confessions since have agreed with it. The page on this site already mentioned describes the view as the church has generally judged it, "as a hope outside its confessions, without contempt for those who hold it." Its hardest questions come from Jesus. He spoke of a sin that "will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come" (Matthew 12:32), and of the shut door and the chasm. A Christian may pray for every person, as Paul tells the church to do (1 Timothy 2:1), and may hope beyond what he has been shown. To teach as certain what Jesus left as a warning is another thing.

## Fair to Whom

The woman's question changes the shape of the problem. A world with no last judgment would be this world left as it is, and the Bible knows what that looks like. "I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness," says the writer of Ecclesiastes, and he reaches the only comfort he can find: "God will judge the righteous and the wicked" (Ecclesiastes 3:16–17). To people who have been safe, judgment sounds like a threat. To her it is the one promise that treats what happened as if it mattered. An account of hell made gentle enough to leave her out has only moved the unfairness onto her.

So the question of what is fair can't be asked only on behalf of the accused. And the son, the student and most of the rest of us ask about hell as people who assume we know which side of the bench we'll be standing on. Paul thought otherwise: "in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things" (Romans 2:1). The psalmist, who wanted justice as much as anyone, prayed, "If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?" (Psalm 130:3). None of that is said against the woman, whose wound was not her doing. It is said to everyone who asks God for strict fairness without thinking what it would find in him.

## The Unfairness at the Center

The Christian faith rests its case on an event that was not fair at all. "For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God" (1 Peter 3:18). Paul's worry in the third chapter of Romans is the reverse of the student's. He asks how God can be just if he forgives, and he answers that God put Christ forward "so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26).

One man in the Gospels speaks about the fairness of his own punishment, and he is being executed as he speaks. "We are receiving the due reward of our deeds," he says to the criminal on the other cross, "but this man has done nothing wrong" (Luke 23:41). Christians confess that the man he was talking about is the one to whom the Father "has given all judgment" (John 5:22). That is a confession, and it proves nothing to the student. Each of the three answers still leaves part of his sum standing. What the confession changes is who will be doing the judging. The one who decides what is fair is one who took a punishment he had not earned.

We have not handled this teaching the way he did. We have preached hell about people we disliked, and with something near to pleasure. We have announced at gravesides what nobody was given to know. We have been the workers hired at dawn, asking strict fairness for others and mercy for ourselves. Then many of us, ashamed, stopped speaking of judgment at all, and that silence told the woman in the first paragraph that the church had nothing to say about the man with the full funeral.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess together that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, that the judgment will be just and "according to what they had done" (Revelation 20:12), that a person can be finally lost, and that salvation is by grace, in Christ alone. They confess that God has no pleasure in anyone's death.

Between the first two answers, what hell is and whether its suffering is endless is a question of the second order. The weight of the church's history and its confessions lies with the first, Christians who hold Scripture as their authority have argued their way to the second, and this essay takes no side. The third stands where the church has left it, as a hope some Christians hold and not as a teaching the church gives.

No one has been told what becomes of any one person, and that includes the father. A separate essay takes up [those who never hear the gospel](/writing/what-happens-to-people-who-never-hear-the-gospel).

Someone once asked Jesus for the figure. "Lord, will those who are saved be few?" (Luke 13:23). He gave no number. He said, "Strive to enter through the narrow door" (Luke 13:24), and left the question about other people unanswered. So the son is not told about his father. He is told who the Judge is. The woman is told that there will be a judgment, and she is not yet shown it. The student still has his sum. What all three have been given is the character of the one who will decide, and each of them will have to judge whether that is enough to go on.

*"Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?"* (Ezekiel 18:23)

*"If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?"* (Psalm 130:3)
